source: Munoz-Avila, Aha, Rizzo (2025) ChatHTN: Interleaving Approximate (LLM) and Symbolic HTN Planning
finding: A SHOP-style HTN planner (PyHop) asks ChatGPT for a decomposition only when no method applies. Then it goes back to symbolic planning. Every decomposition is followed by a verifier task that checks the task's effects, so any plan returned is sound.
numbers: Three domains (logistics, household robot, search and rescue), gpt-4-turbo, default temperature 1, five tries per test, about $30 per domain. Full domain: 0 LLM calls. Unsolvable problem: no plan returned, as proved. With one method removed, most cases solved in 0 to 2 calls; some needed a second run (e.g. truckTransport: failed after 5 calls, then solved in 2).
quote: any plan it generates correctly achieves the input tasks
limits: Tests show soundness, not accuracy rates. Outputs vary between runs even at temperature 0. Planner is not complete. Infinite loops from LLM tasks needed a visited (state, task) check. Small hand-built domains.
agent_relevance: Direct template for O3: use a known method library first, ask the model only for a missing decomposition, and always check the effect of each decomposition before using it.

source: Munoz-Avila, Aha, Rizzo (2025) ChatHTN, No Model ablation and prompt chaining
finding: Removing all methods (pure LLM planning, 'No Model') gave unreliable plans, and the verifier caught the wrong ones. Two-step prompt chaining (free decomposition first, then map it to primitive tasks) worked better than one big query.
numbers: Table 2 marks full-domain and unsolvable cases as X (no plan) with 3 to 4 LLM calls spent; unsolvable still returned a task sequence from the LLM that was not a solution.
limits: Authors say the chaining benefit was observed while testing, citing Kwak et al. 2024; no controlled number given. Checkmarks in the extracted table were garbled in text, so per-cell outcomes are not all read.
agent_relevance: The LLM always produces a plausible decomposition, even for unsolvable tasks. A verifier step is what separates sound from plausible. Our O3 needs a check per decomposition.

source: Munoz-Avila, Aha, Rizzo (2025) ChatHTN, interaction of model decompositions with hand-made methods
finding: Authors found that LLM-made decompositions interact in unexpected ways with hand-made methods, as seen earlier with learned methods (Hogg et al. 2008). So verifiers were added even to hand-made methods.
numbers: No count given. The reason stated: plans from well-crafted methods were correct without verifiers; adding LLM decompositions broke that.
limits: Qualitative report from the authors only.
agent_relevance: Mixing library methods with model-made methods can break guarantees that the library alone had. Verify at the join.

source: Xu & Munoz-Avila (2025) Online Learning of HTN Methods for integrated LLM-HTN Planning
finding: ChatHTN was extended to learn a generalised, reusable HTN method from each LLM decomposition (not simple caching). This cut LLM calls and often raised the share of problems solved.
numbers: gpt-4-turbo, two domains (logistics: 3 cities, 5 packages per problem; search and rescue: 5 survivors). 10 random problems, one method removed at a time, 3 runs each, learned methods deleted after each instance. Result shown only as bar plots: fewer calls with the learner for every removed method; success lower without the learner when LLM errors repeat.
limits: No exact figures in text, only plots. Handcrafted knowledge base. Missing high-level methods (e.g. searchAndRescue, TPM2) remained hard for both settings. Neither setting reached 100%.
agent_relevance: Supports a growing method library: each successful model-made decomposition is stored as a method, so later steps skip the model. Matches the idea of O3 plus memory.

source: Xu & Munoz-Avila (2025) Online learning, repeated querying risk
finding: Without learning, each new instance of the same task re-queries the model, which raises the chance of a wrong answer. The authors say this explains why success is often lower without the learner.
numbers: Reasoning stated in the paper; supported by the bar plots in Figures 8 and 9.
limits: Explanation, not an isolated test.
agent_relevance: Re-deriving the same decomposition each time adds error risk. Store verified decompositions.

source: Meneguzzi, Buchweitz, Correa, Putrich, Pereira (2026) Hierarchical Task Network Planning with LLM-Generated Heuristics
finding: Nine LLMs wrote search heuristics for an HTN planner (PyTrich) given the domain. The virtual-best set nearly matched the best HTN planner on coverage and used far fewer search nodes.
numbers: Six IPC 2020 total-order domains, 139 problems. Coverage: PANDA RC-FF 134, PANDA RC-LMCut 113, TDG 117, LMCount 118, Claude Opus 4 alone 131, LLM virtual best 131. LLM expanded fewer nodes on 104 of 125 shared problems (83%). Barman-BDI 97% fewer nodes at best.
limits: Virtual best over GBFS, A*, WA*. Gap lies in the Robot domain only (time-outs on 8 largest). Benchmarks are public IPC sets and may be in training data.
agent_relevance: A method library plus a model-written guide for which method to try is feasible. Order of method choice matters.

source: Meneguzzi et al. (2026) LLM-generated HTN heuristics, model variance and failure
finding: Model choice mattered far more than search algorithm. Many generated heuristics were broken.
numbers: 780 candidates over 9 models and 6 domains; 419 passed the local filter; 347 solved at least one problem; 72 failed on every problem (60 of 72, 83%, assumed the wrong state type). Median nodes: Opus 4 1,878; PANDA RC-FF 2,178; Gemini 3 Flash 4,346; Gemini 3 Pro 14,746; Gemini 2.0 Flash about 48,600; Gemini 2.5 Pro about 51,200. Best to worst about 27 times. GPT-4o, Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5 and GPT-5.2 produced working heuristics in only one domain each.
limits: Failures persisted though the prompt named the state format. A generate-evaluate-select loop was needed.
agent_relevance: A generate, test, select loop on a training instance is needed; do not trust the first model output.

source: Puerta-Merino, Nunez-Molina, Mesejo, Fernandez-Olivares (2025) A Roadmap to Guide the Integration of LLMs in Hierarchical Planning
finding: A plain LLM planner fails on hierarchical planning problems. No correct hierarchical decomposition was produced for any problem.
numbers: IPC-2023 total-order HTN track, 614 problems in the benchmark, 15 of 23 domains run, Llama-3.1-Nemotron-70B-Instruct. Feasible plans in about 30% of problems; correct plans 4% (13% of feasible); feasible decompositions 3% correct; zero problems with a correct hierarchical decomposition. IPC winner PandaDealer-agile-lama used for comparison.
limits: Preliminary; one open model; no prompting aids; partial domain set.
agent_relevance: Asking a model to emit the whole hierarchy in one go is weak. Combine with a library and checks (see ChatHTN).

source: Puerta-Merino et al. (2025) Roadmap: taxonomy of LLM roles in hierarchical planning
finding: Proposes a taxonomy of how an LLM can serve in hierarchical planning: roles across the planning life cycle (eliciting the problem, generating the plan, post-processing) and strategies to improve it.
numbers: Taxonomy plus benchmark; no further numbers.
limits: Position paper, early stage.
agent_relevance: Maps where model calls could sit in O3: elicit tasks, propose methods, check results.

source: Prasad et al. (2024) ADaPT: As-Needed Decomposition and Planning with Language Models
finding: Recursive decompose-only-when-the-executor-fails beats iterative ReAct, plan-and-execute and Reflexion on three agent tasks.
numbers: GPT-3.5 test splits, dmax 3 (ALFWorld, WebShop), 4 (TextCraft). ALFWorld overall: ReAct 43.3, Plan-and-Execute 43.3, Try Again 47.8, Reflexion 57.5, ADaPT 71.6. WebShop: ReAct 32.0, P&E 17.0, Reflexion 35.0, LATS 38.0, ADaPT 44.0. TextCraft: ReAct 19.0, P&E 27.0, Reflexion 32.0, ADaPT 52.0.
limits: GPT-3.5 executor; ALFWorld Pick2 and Look types show small or zero gains in some baselines; plan comes from the same or another LLM. Paper claims LLM-call counts comparable to baselines.
agent_relevance: As-needed decomposition is the main working LLM version of HTN ideas: decompose only on failure, to a depth that fits the executor.

source: Prasad et al. (2024) ADaPT depth and executor ablations
finding: Gain grows with allowed depth. Deeper recipes gain more. A strong planner can help a weaker executor.
numbers: TextCraft test: recipe depth 2 ReAct 26.9 to ADaPT 78.2 (mean decomposition depth used 1.9); depth 3: 1.8 to 38.7 (mean depth 2.8). ALFWorld dev, weak executor with atomic skills only: 3.3 to 41.7. Planner/executor mix: GPT-3.5 alone 38.4, with GPT-3.5 planner 58.3; LLaMA-2-70B alone 20.4, with GPT-3.5 planner 43.3.
limits: Depth-4 tasks (11) excluded from the depth analysis. Dev and test splits differ across tables.
agent_relevance: Set decomposition depth by the executor's competence, not by a fixed tree. Planner and executor can be different models.

source: Prasad et al. (2024) ADaPT vs plan-and-execute
finding: A fixed up-front plan (plan-and-execute) can be worse than no plan. Adaptive decomposition fixes that.
numbers: WebShop: plan-and-execute 17.0 vs ReAct 32.0 (15 lower). TextCraft: ADaPT beats plan-and-execute by 25 points (52 vs 27).
limits: GPT-3.5 only in the main tables.
agent_relevance: Rigid decomposition up front is a risk; keep re-planning open.

source: Wang, Wu, Yao, Su (2025) TDAG: dynamic task decomposition and agent generation
finding: Each subtask gets its own generated sub-agent. It beats ADaPT on TextCraft and WebShop.
numbers: TextCraft success: ReAct 19.0, P&S 18.5, P&E 27.0, ADaPT 52.0, TDAG 73.5. WebShop reward/success: ReAct 42.1/29.0, ADaPT 60.0/44.0, TDAG 64.5/45.0.
limits: ItineraryBench is the authors' own set; WebShop gain over ADaPT is small (1 point success).
agent_relevance: Per-subtask specialised prompts may help more than one shared prompt, but the gain on a simple task is small.

source: Wang et al. (2025) TDAG error analysis
finding: Fixed-plan methods suffer cascading task failure: one early error spoils the rest. Dynamic decomposition lowers it.
numbers: Cascading-failure share in ItineraryBench (Table 3): ReAct 32.61%, P&E 34.78%, ADaPT 19.57%, TDAG 4.35%, P&S 8.70% (percent of all errors of that type, split across methods).
limits: Own benchmark; shares are relative across methods.
agent_relevance: Check partial progress after each subtask so errors do not cascade.

source: Gui et al. (2025) HyperTree Planning: Enhancing LLM Reasoning via Hierarchical Thinking (ICML 2025)
finding: A hypertree (AND/OR task outline, like an HTN) that the model expands and prunes lifts planning success sharply over CoT, ToT, LATS, RAP and others.
numbers: GPT-4o success: TravelPlanner CoT 4.4 vs HTP 20.0; Blocksworld 35.5 vs 54.7; Mystery Blocksworld 0.0 vs 8.7; Trip Planning 15.6 vs 36.9. Gemini-1.5-Pro HTP: TravelPlanner 36.1 (EvoAgent 8.9, 4.06 times), Blocksworld 67.2, Trip 42.8. Abstract: 3.6 times o1-preview (10.0) on TravelPlanner. Cost about 13% of o1-preview for similar accuracy.
limits: Authors' own comparisons. Table text was garbled in extraction; column mapping read from table order.
agent_relevance: Task trees with explicit sub-task and constraint separation are a working scaffold for long planning.

source: Gui et al. (2025) HyperTree ablations
finding: Dropping the division step hurts TravelPlanner most. A planning outline beats a fixed example hypertree.
numbers: TravelPlanner success (Gemini): full 36.1, without division 7.2, without self-guided 18.9, without outline 30.6. GPT-4o Blocksworld: outline 54.7 vs fixed-example hypertree 43.3. HTP success stays steady as trip length grows while HiAR-ICL, EvoAgent and LATS fall.
limits: Pruning strategy had minimal effect on TravelPlanner; effect seen only on Blocksworld and Trip.
agent_relevance: The split into sub-tasks is the active ingredient. Pruning detail matters less.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in Large Language Models (ICLR)
finding: Solving a task by first listing simpler subproblems, then solving them in order, generalises to harder problems than the examples.
numbers: SCAN length split, code-davinci-002: standard 16.7, chain-of-thought 16.2, least-to-most 99.7. text-davinci-002: 6.0, 0.0, 76.0. code-davinci-001: 0.4, 0.0, 60.7. DROP non-football: CoT 74.77 vs LtM 82.45; football 59.56 vs 73.42. GSM8K: CoT 60.87 vs LtM 62.39.
limits: Prompts are hand-written per task; GSM8K gain is small. Authors note DROP is easy to decompose.
agent_relevance: Decomposition helps most where the test is harder than the examples; gain is tiny when steps are already easy.

source: Khot et al. (2023) Decomposed Prompting: A Modular Approach for Solving Complex Tasks (ICLR)
finding: Separate prompts per sub-task, called by a decomposer, beat one chain-of-thought and least-to-most, and stay near 100% as input grows.
numbers: String-split task: DecomP near 100% on longer sequences, CoT approaches drop (100 examples per set). Multi-hop QA, 300 dev questions: figure values about 64.1 with decomposition-based retrieval vs about 47 to 50 without for code-davinci-002; Flan-T5-XXL about 63.3 vs 49.9.
limits: QA figure values read from text extraction, approximate. Needs hand-built sub-task prompts and a retriever. Decomposer still needs GPT-3-sized models (authors' note).
agent_relevance: A library of callable sub-prompts is the LLM form of HTN methods. Cleanly separated sub-tasks reduce error on hard sub-steps.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2022) PlanBench: An Extensible Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Planning and Reasoning about Change
finding: Base LLMs are weak at generating plans, even in Blocksworld; auxiliary tasks like replanning are easier.
numbers: Blocksworld, 600 instances per task. Plan generation GPT-4 206/600 (34.3%) vs Instruct-GPT3 41/600 (6.8%). Replanning rows 76.8% vs 77.8% and 87% vs 77.8%. Plan generalisation 58% vs 60.5%.
limits: Table layout garbled in extraction, so the mapping of rows to tasks is approximate. Plain prompts with no scaffold.
agent_relevance: Gives the unscaffolded baseline against which a decomposition scaffold should be measured.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) Position: LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks
finding: Names HTN task-reduction schemas as the kind of planning knowledge that LLMs supply approximately. Says many papers confuse that knowledge with executable plans. Proposes an LLM generate plus external critics loop.
numbers: Argument paper; no new experiment.
limits: Position paper.
agent_relevance: Supports pairing the model's guessed decompositions with a sound external check.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with LLMs
finding: A growing library of verified, reusable skills (code) works like a learned method library; removing it stalls progress.
numbers: Versus prior SOTA: 3.3 times more unique items, 2.3 times longer distances, tech-tree milestones up to 15.3 times faster. Diamond tool: Voyager 102 iterations (1/3 runs); w/o skill library, ReAct, Reflexion, AutoGPT none (0/3). Wooden/stone/iron tool: 6, 11, 21 iterations vs 7, 9, 29 without the library.
limits: Single environment (Minecraft), 3 runs per row, GPT-4. Library speed-up at early levels is small.
agent_relevance: Skills are stored only after the task is confirmed done. Same gate for our method library.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried, Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Induce reusable routines (workflows) from past successful runs and show them to the agent. These are learned methods.
numbers: WebArena: 51.1% relative success gain over BrowserGym baseline (12.0 absolute points); 7.6% relative above human-written workflows (SteP). Mind2Web: 24.6% relative step success gain. Gap to baselines grows 8.9 to 14.0 absolute points as train-test distance widens.
limits: Web tasks only. Authors observe agents resist using newly added actions (in 18.5% of tasks).
agent_relevance: Learning methods from experience improves transfer; a method library can be built in use.

source: Erdogan et al. (2025) Plan-and-Act: Improving Planning of Agents for Long-Horizon Tasks
finding: A separate planner writes high-level steps, an executor performs them, and the plan is rewritten after each step. Replanning matters.
numbers: WebArena-Lite (165 tests): baseline 9.85%, 14.21% with a static planner; final system 57.58% (abstract) after synthetic plan data, dynamic replanning and CoT; 81.36% on WebVoyager text-only.
limits: Gains come mostly from fine-tuning on synthetic plan data, not from prompting; static plan is weak because content is unknown ahead of time.
agent_relevance: Plan, execute, replan beats a fixed decomposition. Prompt-only gains are small.

source: Aghzal, Stein, Yao (2026) Why Do LLM-based Web Agents Fail? A Hierarchical Planning Perspective
finding: Splits agents into plan, execute, replan layers (the HTN layers). Models plan roughly in line with humans but execute poorly.
numbers: Mind2Web-Live test, 104 tasks. High-level plan steps matching human subgoals: natural language 60.6%, PDDL 67.7%. NL steps over-decomposed 29.5%, missing 4.2%, unmatched 29.4% (PDDL unmatched 15.4%). Executor with human plans: 38.5% plan completion, 36.4% final success (gpt-5-nano). Decomposition made 68% (NL) and 73% (PDDL) of non-executable subgoals executable, but splitting compact subgoals can hurt.
limits: Headline numbers use one executor (claude-haiku-4.5 29.2%, gemini-flash-2.5 17.3% with human plans). Single benchmark.
agent_relevance: Good plans are not enough. Structured (PDDL-like) task forms are more compact. The bottleneck is grounding at the lowest level.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: Reasoning models collapse on puzzles past a complexity level, even when given the algorithm.
numbers: Tower of Hanoi, Checker Jumping, River Crossing, Blocks World. Giving the solution algorithm did not move the collapse point in Hanoi and Checker Jumping. Near-perfect at Hanoi N=5 (31 moves); Hanoi N=10 fails within the first 100 moves.
limits: Disputed by others as partly an output-length effect; authors answer that failures occur within context limits. Not an HTN test, but Hanoi is a textbook recursive decomposition.
agent_relevance: Knowing the decomposition is not the same as executing it. A scaffold must carry the steps, not rely on the model to keep them.

source: Liu et al. (2023) LLM+P: Empowering LLMs with Optimal Planning Proficiency
finding: Translate to PDDL and let a classical planner solve; the model only does the translation.
numbers: Success rates: Blocksworld LLM+P 90, plain LLM 20; Storage 95 (100 with lenient alias); Termes 85; Barman 20 (100); Tyreworld 20; Floortile 0. Planner: Fast Downward.
limits: Needs a human-written domain file and one example problem. Cell mapping read from a garbled table.
agent_relevance: Handing search to a sound solver after translation is another way to get guarantees.

source: Xie et al. (2024) TravelPlanner
finding: Long, multi-constraint planning breaks plain language agents.
numbers: Final pass rate: GPT-4-Turbo with ReAct 0.6%; all other LLMs 0%.
limits: Benchmark paper; prompts only.
agent_relevance: Shows the size of the gap that decomposition scaffolds like HTP report closing (20.0% to 36.1%).

source: Wang et al. (2024) Planning In Natural Language Improves LLM Search For Code Generation (PlanSearch)
finding: Searching over natural-language plans before code improves diversity and pass rate.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet on LiveCodeBench: PlanSearch pass@200 77.0%, repeated sampling pass@200 60.6%, no search pass@1 41.4%.
limits: Not HTN specific; a plan-level search.
agent_relevance: Searching over plan outlines beats searching over final answers for the same budget.

source: Erol, Hendler, Nau (1994) HTN Planning: Complexity and Expressivity
finding: HTN planning is more expressive than STRIPS operators and undecidable under a mild set of limits. What non-primitive tasks may do affects cost more than variables or ordering.
numbers: Undecidable even with no variables if a task network has two unordered non-primitive tasks. Decidable when either non-primitive tasks or ordering are restricted.
quote: HTN's are more expressive than STRIPS-style operators.
limits: Theory; read from the AAAI-94 text.
agent_relevance: A method library is not just a speed-up: the method set defines what can be solved. Keep recursion and ordering limited.

source: Alford, Bercher, Aha (2015) Tight Bounds for HTN Planning
finding: Gives exact complexity classes for HTN planning by recursion type, ordering and variables.
numbers: No recursion, total order, no variables: PSPACE. Tail recursion with total order and no variables: PSPACE. Partial order or variables push to NEXPTIME, EXPSPACE or 2-NEXPTIME (Table 1).
limits: Read from the first page's Table 1 only, in extracted text.
agent_relevance: Total-order, non-recursive method libraries stay cheap to solve.
